summary.title: Sterile flight deck rule - Wikipedia
summary.one_liner: The sterile cockpit rule limits flight crews to safety-essential activities during critical phases of flight (below 10,000 ft), and the page explains its origins, US regulation, and flight attendant communication issues.
keywords: why pilots cannot talk during takeoff and landing
takeaways: The sterile cockpit rule restricts flight crews to duties needed for safe operation during critical phases, normally below 10,000 ft.
The FAA imposed the rule in 1981 after accidents such as Eastern Air Lines Flight 212 (1974) and Air Florida Flight 90 (1982) were linked to distraction.
In the US, the rule applies to Part 121 and Part 135 operators, not Part 91 general aviation; critical phases include taxi, takeoff, landing, and flight below 10,000 ft except cruise.
The rule can make flight attendants hesitant to call the cockpit, even in emergencies; the FAA and Japan Airlines issued guidance to counter this confusion.
The page lists many crashes attributed to violations of the rule, such as Colgan Air Flight 3407 and Comair Flight 5191.
summary.summary: The Wikipedia article defines the sterile flight deck (sterile cockpit) rule, which bans non-essential activities in the cockpit during critical phases of flight, normally below 10,000 ft. It traces the rule's origin to FAA action in 1981 after accidents caused by crew distraction, and it describes the NTSB findings for Eastern Air Lines Flight 212 and Air Florida Flight 90. The page quotes the US Federal Aviation Regulations (FAR 121.542/135.100) to show what duties and activities are restricted, and it covers the rule's effect on flight attendant-to-pilot communication. It ends with a list of accidents linked to rule violations and further reading.
